question: What do the first five verses affirm about the Word: where it was, with whom it was and what it did?
The term λόγος (logos, “word”) opens the Gospel: what changes when the text says this Word “became flesh and made His dwelling among us”?
John the Baptist first says what he is not and only then what he is: why does the evangelist give so much room to his testimony about Jesus?
Andrew and Philip, after meeting Jesus, go after someone close to them: to whom would you like to say “come and see”?
Who is at the wedding in Cana, what runs out, and through what stages does the water pass before reaching the master of the banquet?
John calls the miracles σημεῖον (semeion, “sign”): where does a sign point, beyond itself, according to verse 11?
What relationship does the evangelist establish between the temple in Jerusalem and the body of Jesus, and why did the disciples only understand later?
Jesus “did not entrust Himself to them,” even with those who believed because of the signs: what sustains your faith when nothing extraordinary happens?
Under what circumstances does Nicodemus seek Jesus, and how does he react to the words about being “born again”?
The verb γεννάω (gennao, “be born, beget”) is repeated in the conversation: what contrast does Jesus draw between what is born of the flesh and what is born of the Spirit?
Why does Jesus compare His mission to the serpent lifted up by Moses in the wilderness, and how does the image of light and darkness explain the “verdict”?
John the Baptist says “He must increase; I must decrease”: in what area of your life would this phrase be a challenge?
What barriers between Jesus and the Samaritan woman does the text itself record at the beginning of the encounter?
The verb προσκυνέω (proskyneo, “worship”) dominates the dialogue: what does Jesus shift in the discussion about the mountain and Jerusalem when He speaks of worshiping “in spirit and in truth”?
What relationship is there between the “food” Jesus speaks of to the disciples and the fields “ripe for harvest”?
The official “took Jesus at His word” and went home before seeing his son healed: what is it like for you to trust without having seen the result yet?
How long had the man been ill beside the pool, and what does he answer when Jesus asks if he wants to get well?
Why does the phrase “My Father is working until now, and I am working as well” increase the hostility instead of ending the discussion about the Sabbath?
The verb μαρτυρέω (martyreo, “testify”) appears many times: what testimonies does Jesus present in His favor, and why do they matter in the debate?
Jesus says it is possible to search the Scriptures and not come to Him: what can make your Bible reading an encounter, and not merely a study?
How do Philip and Andrew assess the resources available before the crowd, and what is left over after everyone eats?
The crowd asks for a sign like the manna: what difference does Jesus point out between the bread the fathers ate in the wilderness and the “bread of life”?
The word σάρξ (sarx, “flesh”) returns insistently at the end of the discourse: how do the Christian traditions usually read the words about eating the flesh and drinking the blood?
When many turn back, Peter asks “to whom would we go?”: what keeps you close when a word seems “hard”?
What do Jesus' brothers propose to Him before the Feast of Tabernacles, and how does He answer them?
The word παρρησία (parresia, “openly, frankly”) appears three times: who speaks openly in the chapter and who keeps silent out of fear?
On the last day of the feast, Jesus speaks of “streams of living water”: how does the evangelist's comment in verse 39 guide the reading of this image?
Nicodemus recalls that the Law hears the accused before judging him: in what situation do you need to listen before forming an opinion?
What accusation do the scribes and Pharisees bring against the woman, what does Jesus do while they insist, and who goes away first?
The word ἀλήθεια (aletheia, “truth”) appears several times: what link does Jesus make between abiding in His word, knowing the truth and being free?
Why does the phrase “before Abraham was born, I am” lead the hearers to pick up stones, and how is it linked to the other “I am” sayings in the chapter?
“Whoever among you is without sin, let him be the first to cast a stone”: how does this sentence change the way you look at another person's wrongdoing?
What do the disciples ask when they see the man blind from birth, and what steps does he follow until he comes back seeing?
Compare how the man refers to Jesus in verses 11, 17, 33 and 38: what does this change show as the interrogations grow harsher?
The verb βλέπω (blepo, “see”) returns at the end of the chapter: what does Jesus mean when He speaks of the blind who come to see and of those who say “we see”?
“One thing I do know: I was blind, but now I see!”: what could you tell, with this simplicity, about your own experience with God?
How does the shepherd differ from the thief and the stranger in the parable, and why do the sheep follow one and not the other?
The verb τίθημι (tithemi, “lay down, give”) is repeated when Jesus speaks of His own life: what do verses 17 and 18 say about the freedom with which He does this?
At the Feast of Dedication they ask Jesus to speak “plainly”: why does He point to His works, and how do the hearers understand “I and the Father are one”?
“My sheep listen to My voice”: how do you try to distinguish this voice among so many others around you?
On receiving the news that Lazarus is sick, what does Jesus do, and how do the disciples react to the idea of returning to Judea?
Martha believes in the resurrection “on the last day”: what changes in the conversation when Jesus says “I am the resurrection and the life”?
The verb πιστεύω (pisteuo, “believe”) runs through the chapter: who is called to believe, at what moment, and what happens afterward?
Caiaphas says it is better “that one man die for the people”: what meaning does the evangelist see in these words, beyond the political intention of the one who said them?
Jesus weeps before the tomb, even knowing what He is about to do: what does this scene say to you about the way God draws near to pain?
What does Mary do at the dinner in Bethany, what objection does Judas raise, and how does Jesus interpret her gesture?
The arrival of some Greeks who want to “see Jesus” leads to the image of the grain of wheat: why does precisely this moment mark that the hour has come?
The verb δοξάζω (doxazo, “glorify”) appears linked to Jesus' “hour”: what kind of glory does the chapter associate with the approaching death?
Some of the leaders believed, but did not confess it out of fear: in what place or group does others' opinion weigh more for you than it should?
At what moment of the supper does Jesus wash the disciples' feet, what does He do step by step, and why does Peter resist?
The verb ἀγαπάω (agapao, “love”) defines the “new commandment”: what is new about it, if love of neighbor was already in the Law?
How does the evangelist tell of Judas's departure, and what weight does the final remark “and it was night” carry?
Jesus says He gave an “example” by washing feet: what quiet service, without position or applause, could you take on this week?
What questions do Thomas and Philip ask Jesus, and what do these questions reveal about what the disciples still did not understand?
Jesus calls the Spirit παράκλητος (parakletos, “Advocate, one called to stand alongside”): what roles does the chapter assign to Him?
How does the phrase “I am the way and the truth and the life” answer Thomas's doubt, and how do the Christian traditions usually understand its reach?
Jesus says He gives peace “not as the world gives”: what difference do you see between this peace and the calm that depends on everything going well?
Who is the vine, who is the vinedresser, and what happens to the branches that do and do not bear fruit?
The verb μένω (meno, “remain, abide”) is repeated many times: what does it mean to remain in Jesus, according to what the chapter itself says?
What difference does Jesus make between calling the disciples servants and calling them friends?
Why does Jesus prepare the disciples for the world's hatred right after speaking so much about love?
“Apart from Me you can do nothing”: in what activity do you usually act as if you depended only on your own strength?
What difficulties does Jesus announce to the disciples, and why does He say it is “to your advantage” that He go away?
According to verses 8 to 15, what will the Spirit do with regard to the world and what will He do with regard to the disciples?
The word λύπη (lype, “grief, sorrow”) appears together with the image of a woman in labor: what does this image suggest about the relationship between sorrow and joy?
“In the world you will have tribulation. But take courage”: what affliction of yours needs to hear this sentence today, and how does it sound to you?
For whom does Jesus pray in each part of this prayer, and what does He ask first for Himself?
What tension is there in being “in the world” without being “of the world,” and why does Jesus not ask that the disciples be taken out of it?
The verb ἁγιάζω (hagiazo, “sanctify”) appears linked to truth and to the word: what does it mean to be sanctified, according to these verses?
Jesus prays for those who would believe later, “that all of them may be one”: what does this prayer ask of you regarding Christians of other churches and traditions?
How does Jesus present Himself to those who come to arrest Him in the garden, what happens when He says “I am He,” and what does Peter do?
The evangelist interweaves Peter's denials with Jesus' interrogation: what contrast does this way of telling the story create?
The word βασιλεύς (basileus, “king”) dominates the dialogue with Pilate: what kind of kingdom does Jesus say He has, and why does this leave Pilate not knowing what to do?
Pilate asks “what is truth?” and goes out without waiting for an answer: in what situation do you also avoid an important question?
How many times does Pilate declare that he finds no basis for a charge against Jesus, and what argument of the accusers finally makes him give in?
What is the meaning of the scene in which Jesus entrusts His mother to the beloved disciple, and how do the Christian traditions read this moment?
The verb τελέω (teleo, “finish, complete”) appears twice in these verses: what would be declared finished in the words “It is finished”?
Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus were secret disciples: what changes in them when they decide to care for Jesus' body?
The sign over the cross was in Hebrew, Greek and Latin: for whom, in your circle, does the story of the cross still need to be “translated”?
Who reaches the tomb first, who goes in first, what does each one see inside, and what is the other disciple's reaction?
Mary does not recognize Jesus when she sees Him, but recognizes Him when He calls her by name: what does this scene suggest about how the Risen One is recognized?
The verb πιστεύω (pisteuo, “believe”) closes the encounter with Thomas: what relationship does Jesus draw between seeing and believing, and whom does He call blessed?
The evangelist says why he wrote this book: how does this purpose help us reread the “signs” told since chapter 2?
The disciples were behind locked doors out of fear when they heard “peace be with you”: what doors do you keep locked today, and what would this greeting say to them?
What happens in the night fishing, how does the beloved disciple recognize Jesus, and what awaits them on the shore?
In the questions to Peter the verbs ἀγαπάω (agapao) and φιλέω (phileo, “love, have affection for”) appear: how do scholars discuss this alternation, and what may or may not it indicate?
What connection might there be between the three questions “do you love Me?” and Peter's three denials told in chapter 18?
Peter asks about the other disciple's fate and hears “what is that to you? You follow Me”: in what do you compare yourself with others instead of tending to your own path?
